Acceptance does not mean that consent needs to be present, but that the securitizing actor must be seen to argue its case to a relevant audience (Buzan et al. 1998, 25). Views on the role and nature of the audience diverge widely in securitization studies. As a definitional matter, audience and referent object are not coterminous— even though they might overlap. A securitizing actor may wish to secure the general population (as in a pandemic) and in that instance audience and referent are essentially the same. In other cases (protecting a group defined by gender, race, religion, or some other categorization), the referent would be more narrowly defined than the audience (drawn from the broader population) to whom the speech act is directed. Views also differ on how significant the audience is to the securitization process. Many scholars believe that the audience (in a liberal democracy this would be the electorate) is the medium through which an extraordinary policy response is legitimized (Cotė 2016). Others (Floyd 2016) largely discount the role of audience because, it is argued, the relevant securitizing actor is often able to act without audience consent (as in cases of unpopular military intervention, for instance). Here, the focus is more on the consequences of securitization than on the precise mechanism of its construction in language.

In spite of the label, securitization theory does not qualify as a ‘theory’, if such a thing is seen as containing a causal relation, general laws, and/ or prediction. However, if theory is regarded as a mechanism to further our scientific understanding, and if science, in line with critical realists, is understood by its content and not its mode of generation (Wight 2006, 24), securitization theory is a theory after all. By using securitization theory, analysts are able to study who can securitize, on what issues, to what effect, and under what conditions (Buzan et al. 1998, 27). Security is not tied to military matters only. Securitization occurs across many different ‘sectors’ (the political, economic, societal, and environmental as well as the military) and levels of analysis. Securitization theory takes no view on whether something really is threatening or on whether or not an issue should be securitized. As we shall see, this does not mean that ‘real’ threats cannot be encompassed within securitization analysis. After all,
socially and politically constructed security threats can refer to threats that are real or merely perceived
. Moreover, below I show that the objective existence of threat is pivotal to the moral permissibility of securitization.
